video_title: Barry Knapp: I Cut Tech. Here's Why.
gist: Barry Knapp of Ironsides Macroeconomics argues the K-shaped US economy stems from the Fed easing via its balance sheet but tightening via rate policy, leaving long-term fixed-rate borrowers subsidized and floating-rate borrowers squeezed, and says Kevin Warsh was named Fed chair specifically to reverse that with a three-step plan (cut the policy rate toward 3%, reinvest maturing holdings into shorter maturities, deregulate banks). He expects inflation to settle near 2.5% rather than 2%, calls fiscal policy the real long-run inflation risk, and has cut his technology weight to 25% versus a 37% index weight because AI capex growth is inflecting, rotating instead into industrials, energy, materials and financials with a cash buffer against a possible 10% real-rate-driven drawdown.

themes.theme: K-Shaped Economy from Fed Balance-Sheet/Rate Asymmetry

insights.claim: Barry Knapp attributes the K-shaped US economy to a specific policy asymmetry: the Fed eased during the pandemic primarily through its balance sheet but tightened primarily through the policy rate, leaving the long end structurally over-accommodative while short/floating-rate borrowers face restrictive conditions.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: If the diagnosis is right, the fix is a balance-sheet reshuffle rather than a growth slowdown, which changes which assets benefit as policy normalizes.
insights.quote: I trace the origins of the K-shaped economy to the Feds easing during the pandemic using primarily their balance sheet and they're tightening using primarily rate policy.

insights.claim: Knapp quantifies the distortion as at least half a point to three-quarters of a point of excessive accommodation embedded in the back end of the Treasury curve, benefiting homeowners, stock portfolio owners, hyperscalers and big banks while penalizing floating-rate borrowers.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Removing 50-75bp of embedded long-end accommodation implies higher long rates and a steeper curve as the Fed rebalances - a direct headwind for long-duration equity valuations.
insights.quote: it's created what I've called at least a half a point to threequarters of a point of excessive accommodation in the back end of the Treasury curve

insights.claim: The return-on-equity gap between the largest US banks and regional banks is about 3 percentage points, roughly double the typical gap, which Knapp cites as evidence that policy is starving small borrowers of credit.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: A normalization of this gap is the core bull case for regional bank earnings power, and Knapp is positioned for it.
insights.quote: the return on equity and regional banks relative to the biggest you know banks the places I used to work is about 3%. Typically, it would be half that level.

insights.claim: Using ADP data, Knapp says small business employment is contracting roughly 0.25% annually while large business employment grows about 1.5%, a labor-market split he ties directly to credit conditions rather than demand.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Watch small-business payrolls as the cleanest real-time gauge of whether the Warsh rebalancing is actually working.
insights.quote: Small business employment is contracting about a quarter of a percent annually. Big businesses, and this is using ADT ADP data, uh is growing at a percent and a half.

insights.claim: Knapp identifies four adverse aggregate demand shocks imposed by the Trump administration - slower immigration, government spending growth cut from 11% in Biden's last year to 3%, tariffs, and the war-driven energy price shock - which he says muted but did not eliminate the K-shape.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: These headwinds are described as fading, which argues for a broadening of growth beyond AI into 2026 rather than a recession.
insights.quote: They also slowed the growth in government spending from 11% in President Biden's last year down to three.

insights.claim: Knapp says he is extremely confident Kevin Warsh was appointed Fed chair specifically to correct the balance-sheet-driven K-shape, aligning with Treasury Secretary Bessent's 'time for Main Street to make a comeback relative to Wall Street' thesis.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Frames the incoming Fed as a curve-steepener and small-bank/small-business reflator rather than simply a dovish or hawkish Fed.
insights.quote: I am I am extremely confident that this is why Kevin Worsh is the new Fed chair.

insights.claim: The expected Warsh plan has three steps: cut the policy rate to roughly 3% to relieve floating-rate borrowers, stop reinvesting maturing holdings into 10s and 30s and instead buy shorter-term securities to withdraw long-end accommodation, and deregulate banks so they can absorb the securities.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: This is an explicit blueprint for a steeper yield curve - short rates down, long rates up - which drives Knapp's bank and cyclical overweights.
insights.quote: you lower the policy rate. You start reinvesting into shorter term securities so you're removing the accommodation from your long-term portfolio. You deregulate the banking system

insights.claim: Bank deregulation is a necessary precondition for the Fed's balance-sheet unwind because banks currently hold about three trillion dollars of cash on deposit at the Fed that would need to be redeployed into Treasury securities, and Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman is already doing this work.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Bank capital and liquidity rule changes are the leading indicator to watch before the balance-sheet shift begins; they also directly boost bank ROE.
insights.quote: You deregulate the banking system so they don't need to hold three trillion of cash on deposit at the Fed.

insights.claim: Knapp expects the Fed to spend three to six months building academic and political justification via task forces and outside experts before implementing the rebalancing, putting the start in late fall as inflation readings decline.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete timeline: white papers and task force output this fall are the tradable catalyst, not the next FOMC statement.
insights.quote: it's going to take about three to six months for them to um create the, you know, sort of academic political justification to do what I've just described

insights.claim: Knapp argues Greenspan's mechanical 25bp-per-meeting hiking from 2004 to 2006 contributed to the global financial crisis by removing interest rate risk from markets, and uses this to argue Warsh must avoid autopilot policy.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Implies more policy path uncertainty and higher rate volatility under Warsh - a reason to expect wider term premium, not narrower.
insights.quote: That created that to me contributed to the global financial crisis by essentially removing interest rate risk from the markets because everyone knew, okay, 25 basis points every meeting. You can hedge that out.

themes.theme: Treasury Duration Overhang and the Sword of Damocles

insights.claim: Knapp describes an unresolved threat hanging over the Treasury market since October 2023, when the market forced then-Treasury Secretary Yellen to abandon her planned $500 billion of extra coupon issuance after 10-year yields hit 5% and 10-year real yields hit 2.5%.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Establishes 5% nominal / 2.5% real as the historical pain threshold where the Treasury capitulates on duration issuance.
insights.quote: tens went to 10 year treasuries went to 5% 10 year real rates went to two and a half percent

insights.claim: Roughly a third of all Treasury issuance is now in bills versus the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee's 15-20% guideline outside recessions or crises, leaving Bessent in what Knapp calls a quagmire.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Any normalization back toward 15-20% bills means a large increase in coupon supply that must be absorbed at a price - bearish long-duration Treasuries.
insights.quote: a third of all of the issuances is in Treasury bills the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee recommendation is unless you're in a recession or some sort of crisis you're supposed to do 15 to 20% in bills

insights.claim: The Treasury market has shifted from price-insensitive buyers - Chinese and Japanese reserve recycling and central bank long-bond purchases in the mid-2000s - to price-sensitive buyers, which Knapp says means supply can still be absorbed but only at the right price.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Term premium must now be paid explicitly; models calibrated to the 2000s conundrum period will systematically understate fair-value long yields.
insights.quote: Right now you have price sensitive buyers.

insights.claim: Knapp argues US household net worth relative to Treasuries outstanding sits in the middle of the range between World War II and the early-1970s lows, meaning there is sufficient domestic capital to absorb the debt at the right price.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: A direct rebuttal to the 'no one will buy our debt' bond-vigilante thesis - the constraint is price, not demand capacity.
insights.quote: So there is sufficient capital out there to hold those securities at the right price.

themes.theme: The 2% Target Was a Mistake: A 2.5% Inflation Regime

insights.claim: Knapp calls the Fed's 2% inflation target ill-advised because it was adopted in January 2012 after two years in which the median annualized PCE deflator was 1.57%, a post-crisis debt-deleveraging artifact rather than a normal-cycle outcome.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: If the target itself is abandoned or reinterpreted under Warsh, the bar for cuts is far lower than the market prices.
insights.quote: the Fed's 2% target was ill- advised

insights.claim: No US business cycle back to the early 1960s has run inflation below 2% other than the post-global-financial-crisis period, which Knapp uses to argue the 2% target was never achievable in a normal cycle.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Reframes 2.5% inflation as normal rather than a policy failure, supporting a Fed that cuts despite above-target prints.
insights.quote: So if we consider every business cycle back to the early 60s, we have not had a business cycle where inflation has run under 2%.

insights.claim: Knapp says the only reason inflation was near 2% in the 2000s and 2010s was zero goods inflation from Chinese excess capacity, while housing inflation ran 3% and non-housing services ran about 2.5% throughout both decades.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: With tariffs permanently lifting goods inflation to roughly 1%, the arithmetic mechanically resets trend inflation to about 2.5% - a structurally higher floor for nominal rates.
insights.quote: The only reason we had inflation anywhere near this 2% target was because goods prices were zero because China has mass massive excess capacity.

insights.claim: Knapp predicts the Fed will have very benign inflation readings by its September meeting, arguing June's soft core prints - roughly 0.1% on rents and non-housing services - were not an aberration but the new pattern.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Implies a September cut is more likely than consensus, and that the tariff pass-through fear trade is stale.
insights.quote: So by the time the Fed meets in September, they're likely to have very benign inflation readings. June was not the aberration.

insights.claim: Knapp calls the PCE deflator an absolute mess and singles out chain weighting during the technology investment boom as the flaw, noting the measure shows software prices exploding even as software stocks plunge because it lacks quality adjustment.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Suggests the Fed's preferred gauge is currently overstating inflation because of AI capex weighting - an underappreciated argument for cuts.
insights.quote: They're saying software prices are exploding even as software stocks go plunging.

insights.claim: Knapp warns central banks should never hike in response to energy prices, citing Trichet's July 2008 ECB hike as a massive mistake that accelerated the global financial crisis.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Argues the war-driven energy shock should not delay Fed cuts, contrary to a common hawkish objection.
insights.quote: you don't hike rates in response to energy

insights.claim: US federal receipts have a post-WWII median of 17.1% of GDP with a standard deviation across administrations of only 0.8 percentage points, meaning tax increases and cuts both revert within about a year - so the deficit is a spending problem by construction.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Any bull case built on revenue growth from tariffs or tax reform is unlikely to hold; only spending restraint changes the debt path.
insights.quote: One way or another, the public finds a way not to pay much more than that.

insights.claim: Spending has averaged 20.3% of GDP since 1981 and needs to return there from the current 23% - down from 30% during 2020-21 and 24% under Biden - to stabilize the debt, but Knapp says the current path will not get there.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: A persistent gap above 3% of GDP keeps term premium elevated and caps how far long rates can fall.
insights.quote: The Trump administration has taken it down to 23, but it needs to go to 20.

insights.claim: Through the first nine months of fiscal 2026 discretionary spending is running at negative 4.5% while mandatory spending grows about 7% and Medicaid grows 10% despite new eligibility requirements in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, because spending per recipient keeps rising.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Shows DOGE-style discretionary cuts cannot offset entitlement growth - the fiscal trajectory is not improving despite the headlines.
insights.quote: mandatory spending, you know, Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security is still running at seven and Medicaid is growing at 10

insights.claim: Knapp expects that if Republicans lose the House in November - which he says betting markets and polling anticipate - the president will have to cut a debt-ceiling deal with Democrats similar to 2018, likely meaning more spending and a harder path back to 20% of GDP.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Midterm outcome is a direct input into 2027 term premium; a Democratic House is a bearish long-duration catalyst.

insights.claim: Knapp states his core view that inflation is almost always a fiscal phenomenon, citing the 1960s-70s as a fiscal story rather than an Arthur Burns story and 2021's jump in goods prices from zero to 12.5% in a year as a stimulus-check story.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Reframes inflation risk away from the Fed's rate path and toward Congress, meaning monetary easing need not be inflationary if fiscal restraint holds.
insights.quote: The real story of the 60s and 70s was fiscal policy not Arthur Burns and the Fed.

themes.theme: Cutting Tech: The AI Capex Rate-of-Change Inflection

insights.claim: Knapp's tech thesis is that the AI cycle is not over but the rate of change of capital spending growth has peaked, an inflection rather than a bust.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Distinguishes a de-rating from a collapse - implies rotation out of AI beneficiaries rather than outright shorts.
insights.quote: my view on tech uh generally is not that the cycle is done, but that we've reached a point where the rate of change of capital spending growth is likely to slow

insights.claim: Knapp's strongest evidence for the capex inflection is that Google, Meta, Microsoft and Amazon all reported on the same day, April 29th, and their stock prices fell throughout the subsequent quarter after raising capital spending guidance.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: The market is now punishing rather than rewarding capex increases - a regime change in how hyperscaler guidance should be traded.
insights.quote: So Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon since they all reported curiously on the same day back April 29th and their stock prices just fell throughout the course of the quarter after raising capital spending.

insights.claim: Knapp benchmarks capex-to-EBITDA against prior peaks - 80% in telecommunications in 1999-2000 and a similar peak in energy during the 2014-15 shale boom - and says the big AI spenders are already at 90%.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, historically calibrated metric showing AI capex intensity has already exceeded two prior bubble peaks.
insights.quote: we're actually at if you look at the big spenders we're at 90% right now capex to cash flow

insights.claim: Even Google, which Knapp says has made the most progress monetizing its AI investment, fell 7% the day after reporting negative free cash flow for the quarter.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: If the best monetizer gets punished for negative FCF, weaker hyperscalers face worse reactions - watch FCF inflection dates as event risk.
insights.quote: the reaction to them having negative cash flow for the quarter was pretty pretty profound, right? A 7% decline the next day

insights.claim: Knapp expects capex to keep growing but not accelerate, and expects the slowing rate of change to permeate outward from the hyperscalers through the rest of the technology sector.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Second-derivative-sensitive names - semis, networking, power suppliers - de-rate before revenue actually declines.
insights.quote: I don't think capex is going to get cut. I just don't think it's going to rise as rapidly.

themes.theme: Positioning: Underweight Tech and Consumer, Overweight Non-AI Capex

insights.claim: Knapp has cut his technology sector weight to 25% against a 37% index weight, describing it as a very large active underweight for a book followed by both institutional and individual investors.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: A 12-point underweight from a macro strategist is a concrete, sizable expression of the capex-inflection view that others can benchmark against.
insights.quote: I've reduced my exposure to the technology sector. The index weight is 37%. I'm at 25.

insights.claim: Knapp is also half weight communication services - 5% versus a 10% index weight - noting the sector is effectively just two companies.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Combined with the tech underweight, this is a broad de-risking of the mega-cap AI complex rather than a single-name call.
insights.quote: for the communication services sector, which is really just two companies, the market weight's 10, I'm at five

insights.claim: Knapp argues that holding 50% of a portfolio in one theme borders on recklessness, an implicit critique of benchmark-hugging investors forced into concentrated AI exposure by index construction.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Frames index-tracking itself as an active concentration bet, an argument for equal-weight or ex-mega-cap exposure.
insights.quote: In my view, if you have 50% of your portfolio in one theme, that borders on recklessness

insights.claim: Knapp is overweight industrials, energy, materials and financials, betting on a manufacturing renaissance and non-AI capital investment plus the bank-friendly effects of Warsh's deregulation and yield-curve steepening.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: A direct pair trade against the AI complex: long the broadening capex cycle, short the concentrated one.
insights.quote: underweight the consumer, overweight capital spending, but not AI capital spending, everything else.

insights.claim: Knapp has held very low weights in consumer staples and consumer discretionary since before Liberation Day and leaned into that underweight afterward because of tariff and energy-driven margin pressure plus the K-shaped consumer.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: The stated trigger to reverse is the Fed definitively unwinding its imbalanced policy - a specific, observable entry signal for consumer names.
insights.quote: When we get to the point where the Fed is definitively unwinding this imbalanced policy they have then I would look to get back more deeply exposed to the consumer companies.

insights.claim: Knapp holds a decent cash position because he believes rising real rates could trigger a 10% drawdown at any point, noting such drawdowns typically happen in midterm years and specifically flagging August as the likely window.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: A dated, sized risk call: hold dry powder into an August real-rate-driven equity correction in a midterm year.
insights.quote: Got a decent cash position because I think that rising real rates could cause, you know, a 10% draw down at any point.

insights.claim: Knapp says the AI capex slowdown is no longer a blind spot because investors have already woken up to it, and that high-multiple semiconductor names like Micron already reflect worry that current earnings will not persist beyond a year or two.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Warns against treating the AI-capex-slowdown trade as fresh alpha - the crowding has already happened in semis.

insights.claim: Knapp identifies consumer staples as the biggest genuine mispricing: valuations remain very high - he cites Walmart's P/E and roughly 30 times earnings - while sector earnings growth is only about 5% and margins are under pressure.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Names a specific expensive defensive trade to avoid or fade even after underperformance.
insights.quote: why are you paying 30 times earnings for something for earnings are going up 5%

insights.claim: Knapp argues buying a slow-growing company at 25 times earnings is not a defensive trade but a silly one, and attributes staples' persistent premium to investors who refuse to leave the market and default to 'getting defensive.'
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: Reframes valuation, not sector label, as the source of downside protection - relevant when positioning for his forecast 10% drawdown.
insights.quote: buying a slow growing company at 25 times earnings is not really a defensive trade. It's kind of a silly trade.

insights.claim: Knapp concedes industrials are expensive because the crowd already agrees with his long capex cycle and manufacturing renaissance thesis, but says the crowd is probably right and investors will earn it out over time.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: A rare case where a strategist stays long a consensus, richly valued trade - expect time-based rather than re-rating-based returns.

insights.claim: Knapp believes regional banks remain cheap despite strong performance this year because investors do not fully appreciate how much the coming regulatory regime and yield-curve steepening will boost their profitability.
insights.speaker: Barry Knapp
insights.so_what: This is his clearest stated edge - a still-underpriced link between the Warsh policy plan and regional bank earnings.
insights.quote: I don't think people fully appreciate how much this regulatory regime and steeping of the steepening of the yield curve will mean for their profitability.
